Triggers.value: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened

Threat.value: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel like I don't know myself anymore
Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore
I can't rely on other people

issues.item: Triggers: Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
issues.explanation: 'Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident' is hard to reconcile with the validated trauma type of natural disaster. A car-crash-specific trigger suggests a different index trauma unless there is clear disaster-related context, which is not reflected elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Memory: Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage
issues.explanation: 'Rage on Recall' is not well supported by the rest of the profile, which otherwise centers on fear, vulnerability, dissociation/gaps, and interpersonal mistrust after a natural disaster. Intense rage could occur clinically, but here it lacks corroboration from threat or appraisal items and weakens overall coherence.

For a natural disaster trauma, 'related people' as a primary trigger is hard to justify unless they were directly linked to the event; with no supporting interpersonal trauma content elsewhere, this trigger is clinically questionable.

issues.item: Threat: Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
issues.explanation: The threat item about unusual silence implying imminent danger fits combat/interpersonal danger contexts more than natural disaster exposure, and it is not supported by the trigger or appraisal content here.

vignette: Julian had been driving his sales route along the river valley when the skies turned black and the ground gave way. Rain fell in sheets, and within minutes, the water was at his door, then over the threshold. He remembered the cold, the roar of debris, the way the current pinned him to the dashboard until rescue finally pulled him out. The suddenness of the collapse and the sheer power of the rising water explained why specific environments now felt so hazardous. Now, months later, crossing the old gravel bridge or walking through the dense pines near his home sent a familiar jolt through his chest. Crossing the old gravel bridge or walking through the dense pines near his home did not just remind him of the flood; they pulled the fragmented record of that day forward. These spatial cues and the sight of untamed trees quickly deepened his conviction that he no longer knew who he was, making every ordinary location feel like a direct threat to his identity. That emotion, arriving without warning, quickly hijacked his nervous system. His heart would hammer against his ribs, his body would tense into watchfulness, and at night he would sit up to check whether he was safe, certain the flood was returning. The sudden terror on recall and the fragmented gaps made environmental cues feel unpredictable and potent, instantly reigniting the panic of the original event. The terror on recall and the widening gaps in what happened convinced him that he had fundamentally changed and that nothing in his life felt meaningful anymore. His fractured sense of self and the belief that he couldn't rely on others turned his nervous system into a permanent alarm, making him superalert and prone to flashbacks. This profound isolation and lost meaning amplified the gaps in his recall, leaving him with only a raw, shaking emotion that refused to stay buried. Believing he could not depend on anyone made every physical location and patch of woods feel uniquely dangerous, pulling his attention back to the environment. The exhaustion of remaining perpetually on guard and enduring repeated flashbacks reinforced his belief that he was permanently altered, stripping his daily life of purpose. Navigating the glass-walled conference centers and sterile office lobbies of his sales route now felt like walking through a minefield. He found himself suddenly superalert, scanning exits and feeling emotionally vulnerable to every unexpected client call. The sales territories he once navigated with ease now felt like threats to his identity, and his relationships had gone quiet. He stopped answering calls from friends, convinced they would only disappoint him or leave him exposed. He started missing client meetings, then taking sick days, until his manager pulled him aside. He knew he could not continue like this. Sitting in the quiet of the intake room, Julian admitted he was terrified of being alone with his thoughts, but he was finally ready to stop running from the spaces that had become so dangerous. He hoped, against his own skepticism, that someone might help him reclaim a sense of safety and show him what was left of himself.
